parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Section four.

You will hear part of a linguistics lecture about attempts to invent a universal language.

First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.

Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

Good morning. Welcome back to the series of linguistics lectures. Today, I'll be talking about the idea of inventing a universal language.

What does that mean? Well, most human languages were never invented. Instead, they evolved over time, and the result is, you know, they're irregular and difficult to learn. So for centuries, people have dreamed of inventing a perfect universal language. The early invented languages that did exist were either created by priests to be used for religious purposes or developed to help establish trade between different nations.

Scholars have found evidence that around nine hundred languages have been invented over the centuries in various parts of the world. But the linguist Arika Okrent believes that the exact figure is unclear because she suspects many of these languages are now lost. No record of them survives.

The first really serious attempt to invent a language was made by William Spencer in the seventeenth century. Like so many others, he was frustrated by the irregularities in all existing languages. Accuracy was particularly important for Spencer because he wrote books. His subject was science.

As a result, he wanted to create a language where words had only one meaning, so everyone would understand precisely what they meant.

At first, he thought the only way to do this was instead of using the usual letters of the alphabet, A, B, C, and so on, he tried to substitute numbers for them. However, this attempt failed, mostly because he couldn't describe complex ideas in this way. So Spencer went back to using the alphabet, but he grouped words together in a different way. When his dictionary was published in sixteen sixty-eight, the words weren't classified in alphabetical order. What he'd done was he'd used the same system with which plants were divided up into groups based on their type.

Another important attempt to invent a universal language was made by Ludwig Zamenhof, who was born in eighteen fifty-nine.

Zamenhof's language reflects his own background. He grew up speaking Polish, English, French, German, and Russian. So rather than create a completely new language, he mixed together five or six existing European languages. Then Zamenhof used an interesting technique to help him develop his new language. He used it to write quite a few different songs, and this made his work more enjoyable.

He also thought that most European languages were too complicated, which meant that it was very difficult for people to learn them. Zamenhof wanted to create a more simple language. So for example, he had a single prefix that was used before adjectives or verbs to make them negative, which is obviously much easier than English.

Then finally, he published a book introducing his language to the world in eighteen eighty-seven. Unfortunately, like other invented languages, no one was very interested at first. So again, Zamenhof used an interesting approach.

In order to publicize the completed language, he made a list of everyone he knew and posted a letter to all of them using the new language.

Many people were surprised how easily they could understand it, and the language began to attract attention.

Zamenhof's language was never used all around the world as he had hoped, but still, it's probably the most successful of all the invented languages.

In the twentieth century, an Australian named Bruce Goldie tried something completely different.

Goldie thought that a universal language would be easier to use if the starting point for each word was a picture.

Goldie spent more than twenty years designing his new language and eventually published a book giving all the details in nineteen forty-nine.

He also went on a lecture tour to promote it. But although the general public were often quite interested, much to Goldie's disappointment, his language was ignored by all of the major universities despite frequent attempts to make them interested.

It wasn't until the nineteen seventies that his language had some success. This was in Canada, in fact, where it was used to teach a group of disabled children in a hospital to read. And as a result, Goldie got some recognition for his work.

So what can we say in conclusion? Well, the truth is all attempts to create a universal language have failed, and there are a number of reasons for this. Firstly, most universal languages have been seen as rather technical and plain. They're not good at conveying emotion, so they've never been very popular. Another reason is the spread of English as a global language in the twentieth century, particularly resulting from the film industry in Hollywood.

Then lastly, the type of people who invented the languages began to change. In the past, it had been academics, but more recently, the languages have often been created by writers, usually for entertainment, so they haven't been taken seriously.

All right. Well, there's one other issue I'd like to consider, and that's the use of-

That is the end of section four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

analyses.content: 录音提到早期的人造语言要么被用于宗教目的，要么是为了帮助在不同国家间建立贸易（trade），直接填入即可。
你可能会因为注意力集中在题干已有的 religious purposes 上，而忽略了录音中由 “or” 引出的并列答案，或者把听到的 nations 误填进来。
The early invented languages that did exist were either created by priests to be used for religious purposes or developed to help establish trade between different nations.
录音明确指出斯宾塞写书，而他书的主题是科学（science）。
你可能会听到 books 就想填，但是 books 在题目中已经给出了，你需要往后听他到底写了关于什么主题的书。
Accuracy was particularly important for Spencer because he wrote books. His subject was science.
录音里说他起初尝试不去用常规的字母，而是用数字（numbers）来替代它们，作为语言的基础。
你可能会听到 alphabet 或 letters 就赶紧填上，但录音里明确说的是“代替”（instead of using）字母，所以真正的基础是数字。
At first, he thought the only way to do this was instead of using the usual letters of the alphabet, A, B, C, and so on, he tried to substitute numbers for them.
录音中提到，为了帮助发展新语言，他用这门语言写了相当多的歌曲（songs）。
你可能会觉得 technique 听起来像个答案，但它太抽象了，题目问的是具体“写”了什么，你需要抓住 write 后面紧跟着的物品。
Then Zamenhof used an interesting technique to help him develop his new language. He used it to write quite a few different songs, and this made his work more enjoyable.
录音中举例说，他用一个单一的前缀加在词语前，来让它们变成否定形式（negative）。
你可能会听到 simple 或 easier 被带偏，但题目要求填入的是加上前缀后单词发生的变化，要重点听 make them 后面的词。
Zamenhof wanted to create a more simple language. So for example, he had a single prefix that was used before adjectives or verbs to make them negative, which is obviously much easier than English.
为了宣传这门语言，他用新语言给他认识的所有人寄了一封信（letter）。
你可能会一听到 list 就急着填，但 list 只是个名单，往后听你会发现他真正寄出去（sent）的东西是一封信。
In order to publicize the completed language, he made a list of everyone he knew and posted a letter to all of them using the new language.
录音提到每个词的“起点”是一幅画（picture），这里的“起点”和题目中的“基于”是一个意思。
你可能会因为没听懂 starting point 和 based on 是一回事，导致没反应过来后面的答案词。
Goldie thought that a universal language would be easier to use if the starting point for each word was a picture.
录音提到在加拿大，这门语言被用来教医院（hospital）里的残疾儿童阅读。
你可能会错填成 Canada，但加拿大在题目里已经给出，你需要听的是在这门语言被使用的具体场所。
It wasn't until the nineteen seventies that his language had some success. This was in Canada, in fact, where it was used to teach a group of disabled children in a hospital to read.
录音指出这些语言不擅长传达情感（emotion），“传达”和题目中的“表达”意思完全对应。
你可能会因为不认识 conveying 这个词，导致明明听到了 emotion 却不敢确认并写下来。
They're not good at conveying emotion, so they've never been very popular.
录音里说明，最近这些语言通常是由作家（writers）为了娱乐而创造出来的。
你可能会听到 academics 就直接填，但录音说的是“过去”（in the past）的情况，题目问的是“现在”（now / more recently）是谁发明的。

Then lastly, the type of people who invented the languages began to change. In the past, it had been academics, but more recently, the languages have often been created by writers, usually for entertainment, so they haven't been taken seriously.
